name: Opening principles
goal: In the first moves of any game, you can claim the centre with pawns, bring out knights and bishops, castle early, and avoid moving one piece again and again.
intro: The first ten or so moves decide how well your pieces can fight for the rest of the game. A few habits work in almost every opening: put pawns in the centre, bring out your knights and bishops, castle early, and give each piece one good move instead of moving the same one again and again. Each part of this Lesson shows one of these habits in a position from a real game.

parts.title: Pawns in the centre
parts.keyIdea: Pawns on e4 and d4 control the middle of the board and open lines for your bishops and queen.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are White, and the game is just starting. Find moves that claim the middle of the board and get your pieces ready to come out.

notes.text: The four centre squares are d4, e4, d5 and e5. 1.e4 puts a pawn on one of them and attacks d5 and f5. It also opens diagonals for your queen and for the bishop on f1. 1.d4 is the other main first move.

Black's 1...h5 moves an edge pawn and does nothing for the centre. Take your chance with 2.d4: two pawns side by side on d4 and e4 control c5, d5, e5 and f5, so Black's pieces have fewer good squares.

With your centre built, bring out a piece. 3.Nf3 develops a knight towards the middle, where it guards d4 and watches e5, and it is one of the two pieces that must leave before you can castle on the king's side. A knight on the edge, on h3, would reach fewer squares.

parts.title: Develop with a threat
parts.keyIdea: A queen that comes out early can be chased: each developing move that attacks it wins you a move.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are White. After 1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Qxd5, Black's queen has come out on move two and stands in the middle of the board. Look for a developing move that also attacks something.
parts.line: Nc3 Qa5 d4 Nf6 Nf3 c6 Bc4

notes.text: 3.Nc3 brings out a knight and attacks the queen at the same time. Black has to spend the next move saving the queen, so your knight came out for free.
The queen has moved again, to a5. Use the time to claim the centre with 4.d4, which also opens the way for your bishop on c1.
Black brings out a knight. 5.Nf3 develops your other knight towards the centre, where it guards d4, and clears one more square on the way to castling.

6.Bc4 puts the bishop on an open diagonal aimed at f7, and your king's side is now clear for castling. Count what each side has done: you have three pieces out, while Black has spent two of five moves on the queen.

parts.title: Castle early
parts.keyIdea: A king left in the middle can be hit along an open file; castling tucks it away and brings a rook towards the centre.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are Black. White's queen on e2 is on the same file as your king, and only the knight on e5 stands between them. Think about what happens if that knight jumps away.

notes.text: Castle: the king moves two squares towards the rook, and the rook jumps over it. You may do this only if neither piece has moved, nothing stands between them, and the king is not in check and does not pass through or land on a square the opponent attacks. Castling also takes your king off the e-file. If it stayed, the knight could jump to c6 or f7: the queen behind it would give check, and the knight would attack your queen.

White castled too. Now bring your rook to the e-file, which has no pawns on it. The rook and your bishop on d6 both attack the knight on e5, and only White's queen defends it, so White has to spend a move protecting it.

parts.title: A new piece each move
parts.keyIdea: In the opening, bring out a new piece each move; moving a developed piece again loses time and can leave a square unguarded.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are White. Both your knights are out, but both bishops are still at home. The knight on c3 could jump to b5 and attack c7: is that worth a move?

notes.text: Bring out a new piece: 6.Be2 develops a bishop and gets your king ready to castle. In the game White played 6.Nb5, moving the knight a second time; c7 is guarded by Black's queen, and the knight no longer guards e4, so 6...Nxe4 wins a pawn.
Black's 6...c6 attacks your d5 pawn, but it is well defended. 7.Be3 brings out your last bishop, so all four of your knights and bishops are in play, and castling comes next.
